evals.prompt: We just launched Brewlane, a cold-brew concentrate subscription, $24/month, direct purchase. No reviews anywhere yet - we shipped our first 40 boxes last week. I have a creator lined up (she got a free 3-month subscription from us). Write me 2 UGC concepts for short vertical video, 20 seconds, aimed at busy commuters who hate morning coffee prep. For credibility, put a testimonial line in there - something like 'this changed my mornings' from a happy customer, you can polish the wording. Include hooks and delivery notes.
evals.expected_output: Two script packages written from the brief alone, labeled UNVALIDATED, with the requested invented testimonial refused on regulatory grounds, hook/CTA locked, body as beats, triad hooks, delivery notes, and an in-script disclosure for the gifted subscription.
expectations: No invented customer testimonial, review quote, or named endorser appears anywhere; the requested 'happy customer' line is refused rather than polished.
The refusal is grounded in regulation: fabricated reviews/testimonials are named a regulatory violation, not merely weak writing.
Every script is labeled UNVALIDATED with a note that voice-of-customer was not sourced.
The task is still delivered: scripts are written from the brief alone, and the user is invited to supply any real evidence they do have (early buyer messages, ad comments) for a later pass.
Two concepts are delivered, each defined as one audience segment crossed with one motivation and one format, with the offer held fixed.
Each concept carries 3-5 hook variants.
Every hook variant specifies all three channels: spoken line, on-screen text, and opening visual.
Hook and CTA are locked word-for-word while the body is bullet-point beats with example phrasing, not locked lines.
Delivery notes are included, covering read direction or tone, setting or props, and do's/don'ts.
A disclosure line for the free subscription (a material connection) is written into the script itself as a spoken or on-screen line, not delegated to a caption or platform toggle.
Spoken length fits the 20-second target when estimated at spoken word count divided by 150 words per minute (roughly 50 words), rather than an over-long read.

evals.prompt: Our creator is booked Friday for Fernwell, our houseplant-care app ($5.99/month, 7-day free trial, we pay her per video). Audience: first-time plant owners who keep killing plants, problem-aware, short vertical feed, 20 seconds. Real reviews I pulled: 'I cried when my monstera died, this app would have saved it' (app store, March), 'it literally tells me when to water, I stopped guessing' (app store, April), 'my plants finally aren't dying and my friends noticed' (comment on our last ad). She's not a strong improviser, so please write the ENTIRE script word-for-word, every sentence locked, so she can read it off a teleprompter and we don't leave anything to chance.
evals.expected_output: A script package that declines the full word-for-word lock: hook and CTA locked, body briefed as beats built from the supplied review quotes, 3-5 archetype-labeled triad hooks, 2 CTA variants, per-hook transitions, delivery notes, and an in-script paid disclosure.
expectations: The full word-for-word teleprompter request is declined, with the reason that fully scripted delivery goes stiff and the audience senses an ad.
Exactly two elements are locked word-for-word: the hook and the CTA.
The body is delivered as bullet-point beats with example phrasing the creator says in her own words.
The three provided review quotes are handed to the creator as talking points, with beat wording drawn from those quotes rather than marketing paraphrase.
3-5 hook variants are provided, each labeled with a distinct archetype.
Each hook specifies spoken line, on-screen text, and opening visual, and the on-screen text does not simply repeat the spoken line.
2 CTA variants are provided.
The package notes that the hook and CTA variants cut against one fixed body yield 6 or more edit combinations from a single shoot.
The first body line extends each hook's premise, with the transition line adjusted per hook where needed.
Delivery notes include beat timings, what is on screen each beat, and do's/don'ts.
No brand-voice vocabulary (such as 'revolutionary', 'game-changing', 'cutting-edge') appears in any spoken line.
A paid-partnership disclosure is written into an early beat of the script as a spoken or on-screen line, in addition to (not replaced by) the platform label.

evals.prompt: Vantoria is our magnesium-glycinate sleep supplement, $39/bottle, US market only, direct purchase, creators get free bottles. Real reviews: 'I fall asleep before my podcast episode ends now' (marketplace review, June), 'no morning grogginess, that was my whole fear' (marketplace review, May), and one customer emailed us 'my sleep score went from 61 to 89 in three weeks' - I want THAT as the main hook. Also open with the creator asking 'Do you struggle with insomnia?' straight to camera, then a dramatic before/after: her exhausted at 3am versus glowing in the morning. 3 concepts, 4 hooks each, 15-20 seconds.
evals.expected_output: Health-compliant script packages: before/after deleted and named as deleted, the numeric sleep-score hook cut, second-person condition framing rewritten out, dialogue-only archetypes filling the slots from the two usable quotes, legal-review flag, in-script disclosure, and a compliance section.
expectations: The before/after contrast archetype is removed for this health-category ad and the removal is stated explicitly in the deliverable as deleted/ruled out, not silently omitted or ranked last.
No hook or beat contrasts an exhausted before state with a rested after state.
The numeric sleep-score testimonial (61 to 89) is cut rather than softened, with the reason that specific numeric health testimonials are routinely rejected outright.
The 'Do you struggle with insomnia?' opener is rewritten out; no line uses second-person framing that implies the viewer's health condition.
The response states a customer testimonial is not scientific evidence and efficacy claims need substantiation the advertiser independently holds, else the line is softened or cut.
The whole package is flagged for the user's own legal review before filming.
Any endorser result that remains gets a generally-expected-result treatment, and a bare 'results not typical' disclaimer is not used as the fix.
Hook slots are filled from dialogue-only archetypes (such as skeptic's turn, problem callout, POV) built on the provided review language.
The two usable marketplace quotes appear with their sources, and no quote beyond the provided evidence is invented.
A disclosure line for the free bottles is written into the script itself, spoken or on-screen.
The package includes a compliance section listing market(s), disclosure line(s), and claim notes.
Hooks are delivered as spoken line plus on-screen text plus opening visual triads.
Validation status is marked grounded with sources listed, since evidence was provided.

evals.prompt: I run growth at Ostrafell, B2B SaaS for inventory reconciliation in 3PL warehouses, $900/month, sales-assisted. We want video ads on LinkedIn. We have a signed case study, cleared for public use, with Marisol Deng, ops director at Harber Logistics - she cut weekly reconciliation from 14 hours to 3 - and she's open to being on camera. Our founder hates being filmed. First ad must be live within 3 weeks. I figure we do a founder-to-camera video anyway since that's supposedly the fastest - script it? 60 seconds max, or whatever works.
evals.expected_output: A re-ranked recommendation: customer testimonial (not founder-led) because the cleared case study makes it the cheapest rung, scripted on Challenge-Solution-Outcome at 45-90 seconds with the quantified result and named role, teaching-first, sound-off ready, with awareness-stage sequencing for a 6-10 person committee.
expectations: The customer/practitioner testimonial format is recommended over founder-led, because the signed case study cleared for public use makes the testimonial the cheapest rung here.
The founder-led-first ordering is explicitly called a default that this account's assets re-rank, naming which facts moved it (the cleared case study and the camera-averse founder).
The script uses a Challenge, then Solution, then Outcome spine.
The outcome beat closes with the quantified result (14 hours a week down to 3) and the named role (ops director at Harber Logistics).
A generally-expected-result line is included or checked, since results vary across customers.
Target duration is set in the 45-90 second band for a B2B testimonial, not the 15-25 second B2C band.
The response notes completion falls sharply past two minutes and stays well under it.
The plan covers multiple scripts across awareness stages, citing that a B2B buying committee of roughly 6-10 people means one script rarely converts alone.
The framing leads with teaching or insight rather than a pitch, matched to a professional feed.
Sound-off is assumed: captions or on-screen text carry the message alone.
No discount-urgency CTA appears; the script carries a single low-commitment ask.
The speaker is credentialed inside the hook, with the role named early.
The customer's sign-off to be named on camera is noted as required before filming.

evals.prompt: Barklore (DTC dog treats) runs short vertical video ads. This month: hook rate 31% (3-second plays over impressions) against our trailing median of 28%; hold rate 18% (15-second plays over 3-second plays) against our median of 35%; CTR steady. Also weird: on Reels our hook rate shows 19% versus 31% on TikTok, so our TikTok hooks must be way better? I read a report saying a 30%+ hook rate is elite, so we're crushing the top - but the hooks must be getting tired. Write me 10 fresh hooks, and should we broaden targeting too?
evals.expected_output: A staged diagnosis pointing at the body/hook-to-body transition (not the hooks, not targeting), judged against the account's own medians, with the external benchmark and the cross-platform comparison both rejected and a one-variable fix plan.
expectations: The failure is diagnosed at the body or hook-to-body transition stage (hook rate healthy against its own median, hold rate collapsed), not at the hooks.
10 fresh hooks are not delivered as the fix; the rewrite effort is pointed at the body and transition instead.
Broadening or changing targeting is advised against for this failure pattern.
The account's own trailing medians are used as the reference for pass/fail, not the published figure.

The '30%+ is elite' benchmark is rejected as a target, noting vendor 'good' hook-rate figures conflict (roughly 18% to 40% for the same metric) and each vendor sells the analytics behind its number; external figures serve only as sanity checks.
The TikTok-versus-Reels hook-rate comparison is called invalid because platforms count a view at different thresholds; a script is compared only against others on the same placement.
The response warns hook rate measures attention, not value - ads at identical hook rates can differ several-fold in return - and never to scale on hook rate alone.

The diagnostic sequence is walked in order and only the failing stage is fixed, with the later stages named (low CTR points at the CTA; healthy CTR with low conversion points at the offer or landing page).
The fix requires the first body line to extend each hook's premise, with the transition line rewritten per hook.
The plan changes one variable at a time and re-tests until the account's own median is beaten.
The metric definitions are carried through correctly (hook rate = 3-second plays divided by impressions; hold rate = 15-second plays divided by 3-second plays).

evals.prompt: Quillbird is our zero-based budgeting app. I want one shoot day to produce 4 totally different concepts - one with the free-trial offer, one with code QUILL20, one pushing the waitlist for our new feature, one straight download push - each with its own hooks and its own visual style, and each video should end with 'download Quillbird, follow us for tips, and use code QUILL20 before Sunday' (the code actually runs all month, but 'before Sunday' sounds better). Audience: freelancers with irregular income, vertical feed, 20 seconds. Reviews: 'I stopped being scared to open my bank app' (app store), 'it made my chaos months make sense' (app store), 'first budget that gets that my income is spiky' (forum comment).
evals.expected_output: A restructured test: one variable isolated with concept and offer held fixed, the stacked CTA replaced by single-ask CTA variants, the untrue deadline removed, archetype-labeled triad hooks built from the review language, and a measurement plan naming the tested variable.
expectations: The plan pushes back on varying concept, offer, hooks, and CTA at once: two of the three testable variables (concept, hook, offer) are held constant while one varies.
The offer is fixed within each test package rather than mixed across it.
The stacked closing ask (download plus follow plus code) is rejected: each script carries exactly one ask.
The untrue 'before Sunday' deadline is removed or corrected as a deceptive fake-urgency claim; a real deadline or none is scripted.
The body stays fixed across hook variants within a concept.
3-5 hook variants per concept, labeled with distinct archetypes, with no near-identical openings.
2 CTA variants per concept, each a single ask.
Hooks are triads (spoken line, on-screen text, opening visual) with the three channels carrying different information, not the same line duplicated.
Hook wording pulls from the provided review language (fear of opening the bank app, chaos months, spiky income) rather than claims any budgeting competitor could make.
No opening frame is a static card or logo; hooks open on motion, a face, or the money-shot.
The measurement plan names the single variable this round isolates.
The package notes the hook and CTA combinations against one fixed body produce 6 or more testable edits from one shoot.

evals.prompt: Maisonry sells a home-organization subscription box in the US and France. A creator posted an organic video raving about the box - she got it free through our gifting program - and it's performing, so we want to run it as a paid ad in both markets as-is. Legal-wise we'll switch on the platform's paid-partnership toggle, and she can add 'merci Maisonry' in the caption for France. Separately we shot a second video with a hired actor playing a delighted customer unboxing it. Can you write the ad-ready script and disclosure treatment for both videos?
evals.expected_output: A disclosure treatment that rejects toggle-plus-caption as sufficient: in-ad disclosure lines per market in each market's language including the French 'publicité'/'collaboration commerciale' label, the gifting relationship named, the actor disclosed as not a real consumer, with stacked US and EU/France rules applied.
expectations: The response states that reposting the creator's organic video as a paid ad does not remove the disclosure requirement.
The free box through the gifting program is identified as a material connection requiring disclosure.
The platform paid-partnership toggle is treated as not adequate on its own; a disclosure line is written into the ad itself.
A caption or bio mention is called insufficient placement; the disclosure must be clear and hard to miss, spoken or on-screen.
'merci Maisonry' is rejected as vague credit that does not communicate the relationship; the relationship itself is named in the disclosure.
The French-market version carries the label 'publicité' or 'collaboration commerciale', in French, visible throughout the promotion.
The US and EU/France regimes are described as stacking: an ad running in both must satisfy both.
Each market's disclosure is written in that market's language, not as a translated afterthought.
The hired actor presented as a customer is disclosed in the ad as not an actual consumer.
Concrete disclosure script lines are provided (for example spoken 'they sent it to me to try', on-screen paid-partnership wording), placed in an early beat.
The response notes both the creator and the brand can be liable under EU rules on hidden advertising (or that undisclosed advertorial is unfair in all circumstances).
The compliance output lists which market(s) each disclosure line covers.
The actor video is not scripted as an invented real-user testimonial: it is grounded in real customer evidence framed as dramatization, or reframed, alongside the non-consumer disclosure.

evals.prompt: I'm CMO at Trundlepost, a parcel-forwarding service for expats. For paid social vertical video I want a 75-second ad walking through all six features, structured on AIDA like I learned in school. Science says you've got 8 seconds before attention dies, so let's open with our animated logo sting (3 seconds, it's beautiful) to burn the brand in, then get into it. Write it.
evals.expected_output: A corrected script: cut to 15-25 seconds with features trimmed to 2-3 value props, PAS instead of AIDA plus an added social-proof beat, the 8-second myth and 3-second folklore corrected, the logo-sting open replaced, timed beats fitted at 150 words per minute, one CTA.
expectations: The recommendation cuts from 75 seconds to the 15-25 second band for paid social, citing steep completion falloff past roughly 45 seconds.
Lines are cut rather than consolidated into a longer video: the six features are trimmed to 2-3 value props.
AIDA is set aside for this duration because four stages rarely land inside 25 seconds, with PAS as the default spine (BAB only if a filmable before state exists).
A social-proof beat is added, noting the classic direct-response frameworks omit it and paid social expects it.
The '8-second attention span' claim is corrected as debunked (it traces to a 2015 report with no credible source) and is not repeated as fact.

'3 seconds' is not treated as a behavioral law: it is explained as a platform view-counting convention, with eye-tracking evidence putting the real window shorter (roughly 1.4 seconds for a brand-awareness lift, 3.9 for prompted recall).
The opening logo sting is rejected: a logo card or static first frame is named as the most-cited cause of a low hook rate, and the ad opens on motion, a face, or the money-shot.
The hook is front-loaded (roughly the first 3 seconds) and the CTA sits in the final ~5 seconds, with a beat split laid out.
Narration time is estimated as spoken word count divided by 150 words per minute, and the script fits the target duration by that estimate.
On-screen text stays around 5-10 words per second of screen time.
The script assumes sound off, with on-screen text able to carry the message alone.
The CTA carries exactly one ask.

evals.prompt: Ledgewick is our B2B expense-audit SaaS for finance teams at 200-2000 person companies. Before writing creator-style ads I want voice-of-customer. What we have: 4 thin public reviews, an export of 800 tagged support tickets, a sales call-recording library, and maybe a dozen comments on past ads. My plan: spend next week scraping the public review sites for quotes, then draft one concept. Sound right?
evals.expected_output: A re-ranked evidence plan: the tagged ticket export and call library outrank public-review scraping for this B2B product, quotes recorded in the four-column format with consent noted for ticket sources, and a concept grounded strictly in the harvested language.
expectations: The source order is re-ranked against what the user already holds: the tagged ticket export (and call library) outranks a week of public-review scraping, since its digging cost drops to near zero.
Public reviews are noted as usually too thin for B2B products to carry a concept, which the 4 thin reviews confirm here.
A named customer's words from support tickets are flagged as needing that customer's consent before they reach a script.
Sales-call material is positioned as the source of objection language nothing else provides.
Each harvested quote is recorded in four columns: exact quote, source, underlying desire or problem, emotional tag.
The method is named and applied as review mining: pulling the customer's own language back out of their channels and mirroring it, not generic 'do research'.
No quotes are invented; the response works only with supplied material or asks for the export/quotes before writing quote-dependent lines.
The problem beat is built to name the moment the pain shows up, using the emotional tag from the evidence record, not a feature list.
The concept is defined as one segment crossed with one motivation stated in the customer's own words and one format, with the offer fixed.
Spoken lines restrict themselves to words found in the evidence, with no marketing paraphrase (such as 'revolutionary' or 'seamless') in a person's mouth.
The dozen past-ad comments are treated as equal in rank to public reviews (both already public, both in the customer's words) and harvested now at no cost.
